nameStory: This little succulent gets its name 'thick-leaved stonecrop' from its plump, fleshy leaves that store water like tiny cushions. The 'stonecrop' part comes from these tough plants' amazing ability to grow in rocky crevices and stone walls where almost nothing else can survive. They literally 'crop up' from stones!
description: Thick-leaved stonecrop is a tiny, low-growing succulent that forms dense, cushion-like mats rarely more than 2-3 inches tall. Its small, thick leaves are packed tightly together on creeping stems, giving it an almost moss-like appearance from a distance. This Mediterranean native produces delicate white or pale pink flowers on short stems above the leafy mat. It's extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation in the region.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, egg-shaped leaves that feel thick and squishy like little water balloons, arranged in dense clusters along the stems and often covered with a grayish bloom

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms tight, creeping mats that hug surfaces like a living carpet, spreading outward rather than growing tall

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pale pink star-shaped flowers with 5 petals, appearing on short stalks that rise just above the leaf mat

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels soft and cushiony to the touch, with leaves that give slightly when pressed like tiny pillows

habitat: In its native Mediterranean range, this stonecrop grows on rocky walls, stone buildings, and cliff faces. In New England, if encountered, it would likely be found growing on old stone walls, rock gardens, or possibly escaping from cultivation around buildings. It prefers well-drained, rocky soils and can tolerate very dry conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as temperatures warm, with the thick leaves becoming more plump and green. Early flowers may appear in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering season with small white or pink star-shaped blooms appearing above the leafy mat. The succulent leaves are at their most water-filled and squishy.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall. The plant remains green and active longer than most other plants as it uses stored water in its leaves.
seasonality.winter: Being a Mediterranean plant, it's not reliably hardy in most of New England and may not survive harsh winters, though it might persist in very protected microclimates.

funFact: This tiny plant is so drought-tolerant that it can survive completely without water for months by living off the moisture stored in its plump leaves, which can shrivel to half their normal size and then plump right back up after the first rain!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small stonecrops, but thick-leaved stonecrop has distinctively plump, grayish leaves that feel much more cushiony than the firmer, more pointed leaves of biting stonecrop or the longer, stringy appearance of stringy stonecrop.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Corsican stonecrop' in some references, this plant is actually native to a much broader Mediterranean region. Its extreme rarity in New England means any sighting would be noteworthy and likely represents either a recent introduction or garden escape rather than an established population.
compareHints: Unlike the yellow-flowered biting stonecrop with its pointed, cone-shaped leaves, thick-leaved stonecrop has white or pink flowers and much plumper, rounder leaves. It's also much smaller and more cushion-like than stringy stonecrop, which spreads with trailing stems and has longer, more cylindrical leaves. The grayish bloom on its leaves also sets it apart from most other stonecrops in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike biting stonecrop which has tiny needle-like leaves that taste peppery, stringy stonecrop has larger, flatter leaves in groups of three that are essentially tasteless.
Among New England stonecrops, biting stonecrop has the smallest, most tightly overlapping leaves and the most intense golden-yellow flowers.
Among New England's stonecrops, white stonecrop stands out for its pure white flowers and cylindrical leaves that look like tiny green hot dogs.
Tasteless stonecrop's six-spiral leaf arrangement sets it apart from most other stonecrops in New England.
Woodland stonecrop stands out from its stonecrop relatives by its preference for shade and its unique four-petaled white flowers – most other Sedum species have five yellow petals and love full sun.
Among New England's stonecrops, Spanish stonecrop is distinguished by its particularly dense, mat-forming growth and tendency toward reddish stem coloration.

Mexican Stonecrop stands out from other New England stonecrops by its bright yellow-green 'lemon coral' coloration, while Stringy Stonecrop is more blue-green and Biting Stonecrop has shorter, more tightly packed triangular leaves.

Unlike the common yellow-flowered biting stonecrop or the shade-loving woodland stonecrop with its distinctive three-leaf clusters, cliff stonecrop has pure white flowers and distinctly blue-green (glaucous) leaves.
Makino's stonecrop differs from Stringy Stonecrop by its more compact, less trailing growth habit and smaller stature.
